links.note: 121 says lack of restraint drives one into thick darkness (ஆரிருள் உய்த்து விடும்); 243 says those whose hearts hold அருள் do not enter the painful world joined with darkness (இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம்). Both use darkness as the place a moral failing leads to, which Parimelazhagar glosses in both verses as a hell; the pairing shows the same destination attached to two different virtues, restraint in the householder's section and அருள் in the ascetic's.

121 ends அடங்காமை ஆரிருள் உய்த்து விடும், and 168 ends with envy, called a பாவி, which destroys fortune and தீயுழி உய்த்து விடும். The same closing verb phrase, 'drives and leaves one there', is used for lack of restraint and for envy, so the two vices are given the same power to deliver a person to a bad place.

121 says restraint brings one among the immortals (அமரருள் உய்க்கும்); 50 says one who lives on earth as one should will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப்படும்). Both promise a place among the gods to a person living an ordinary household life well, without renunciation, and 121 names restraint as the quality that does it.

31 asks what gain is greater for a living being than virtue (அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கம் எவனோ உயிர்க்கு); 122 says there is no gain for a living being beyond restraint (ஆக்கம் அதனினூஉங்கு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு) and tells one to guard it as wealth. 122 reuses chapter 4's formula almost word for word and applies it to one particular virtue, so restraint is given the rank the earlier verse gave to virtue as a whole.

122 tells one to guard restraint as பொருள், wealth, since nothing is a greater gain; 363 says there is no fine wealth (விழுச்செல்வம்) here like not wanting, and nothing equal to it there either. Both verses count an inner holding-back as the real wealth and both use the 'nothing equals it' form, once for the householder's restraint and once for the renouncer's freedom from craving.

123 says that if one knows and then restrains oneself in the proper way (அறிவறிந்து ஆற்றின் அடங்கப் பெறின்), that restraint is recognised and yields distinction; Parimelazhagar takes அறிவறிந்து as knowing that restraint is itself what knowledge is. 834 gives the negative: no fool is greater than one who has studied, understood and taught others but is not himself restrained (தானடங்காப் பேதை). Together they say knowledge is finished only when it turns into restraint.

123 calls restraint செறிவு and says that, recognised, it yields distinction; 715 calls not speaking first among elders a செறிவு and ranks it the best of good things (முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு). The shared word shows the general restraint of chapter 13 turning up in the assembly as a concrete act, holding back one's speech before those who know more.

124 says the stature of one who is restrained without shifting from his station (நிலையின் திரியாது அடங்கியான்) is far greater than a mountain's. 965 says even those like a hill will sink if they do a lowering thing as small as a kundri seed (குன்றின் அனையாரும் குன்றுவர்). The mountain stature of 124 holds only while the 'not shifting' holds; 965 states how little it takes to lose it.

124 praises one who is restrained and does not shift from his station (நிலையின் திரியாது); 989 says those called the ஆழி of worth do not shift even when the age shifts (ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம் பெயரார்). Both measure a person by immovability, 124 against a mountain and 989 against the turning of an age.

29 speaks of those who have climbed and stand on the hill called good qualities (குணமென்னும் குன்றேறி நின்றார்), whom Parimelazhagar takes to be ascetics; 124 says the restrained person's stature is greater than a mountain (மலையினும் மாணப் பெரிது), and Parimelazhagar reads நிலை there as the householder's state. On his readings the renouncer stands on a hill while the householder who stays restrained in his own station is said to overtop one.

125 says bowing (பணிதல்) is good for everyone and is a further wealth for the wealthy; 963 says bowing is needed in abundance (பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல்) and standing tall is needed in shrunken circumstances. 963 keeps 125's point about the rich and adds the other half: when one has little, the same concern for character calls for not stooping.

125 says bowing is good for all and especially fine in the wealthy; 978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை) while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration. Both make humility the mark of those who have most reason for pride, wealth in one verse and greatness in the other.

125 treats bowing (பணிதல்) as an excellence, a second wealth for the rich; 985 says bowing is the strength of those who get things done and the weapon by which the worthy turn opponents around (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பணிதல்). The same act is valued as character in the Book of Virtue and as effective power in the Book of Wealth.

126 says that drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is a protection through seven (ஒருமையுள் ... எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து); 398 says the learning one gains in one birth is a protection through seven (ஒருமைக்கண் ... எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). The closing formula is identical, so sense-restraint and learning are set side by side as the two acquisitions that carry across births.

126 says restraint of the five in one birth protects through seven; 835 says a fool can, by what he does in one birth (ஒருமைச் செயல்), make the mire he will sink in through seven (எழுமையும் தான்புக்கு அழுந்தும் அளறு). The one-birth and seven-births arithmetic runs in both directions: one life is enough to secure the next seven or to ruin them.

126 pictures restraint as a tortoise drawing in its five (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்); 24 pictures it as guarding the five with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்), which Parimelazhagar explains as driving five elephants. The two animal figures show two sides of the same control: the senses as limbs to be withdrawn from danger and as strong beasts to be steered.

127 says whatever else they fail to guard, let them guard the tongue, or they will grieve through a fault of speech (நாகாக்க காவாக்கால் சோகாப்பர்); 305 says if you would guard yourself, guard against anger, or anger will kill you (சினங்காக்க காவாக்கால் தன்னையே கொல்லும்). The sentence frame காக்க / காவாக்கால் is the same, and in both the harm of the unguarded thing falls on the person who failed to guard it.

127 warns that an unguarded tongue brings grief through a fault of speech (சொல்லிழுக்கு); 642 tells the minister to guard against any lapse in speech (காத்தோம்பல் சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு) because both gain and ruin come from it (ஆக்கமும் கேடும்). 642 carries the rule into statecraft and adds what 127 leaves out: speech is guarded not only because it can harm but because gain comes by it too.

128 says that if even one bad word has its effect, the good turns out not good (ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல் ... நன்றாகாதாகி விடும்); Parimelazhagar takes this as the person's other merit turning bad. 965 says even hill-like people sink if they do a lowering thing the size of a kundri seed. Both hold that a single small lapse is enough to cancel a large standing good, in speech in one verse and in honour in the other.

128 says one harmful word undoes a person's good; 109 says that even a hurt as bad as killing vanishes when one thinks of a single good the person did (அவர்செய்த ஒன்று நன்று உள்ளக் கெடும்). The 'one outweighs all' logic is used in opposite directions: in judging one's own speech one bad instance spoils everything, and in judging someone who has helped you one good instance clears everything.

129 says a wound burned by fire heals within but a scar burned by the tongue does not (தீயினாற் சுட்ட புண் உள்ளாறும்); 896 says one burned by fire may still survive, but those who go on offending the great will not (எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம்). Both use a burn as the injury one can recover from, in order to mark something worse: a spoken wound in 129 and the anger of the great in 896.

129 sets a fire-burn, which heals, against the tongue's scar, which does not; 1049 says one can even sleep in the middle of fire but cannot close an eye in the middle of poverty (நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும்). The book repeatedly takes fire as the measure of bearable pain and places a non-physical hurt beyond it.

129 says the scar left by the tongue never heals; 159 says those who bear the harsh words from the mouths of people who exceed all bounds (இறந்தார்வாய் இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்கிற்பவர்) are as pure as renouncers. 129 gives the reason 159's praise is so high: what the forbearing person takes without retaliation is the one kind of wound the book says does not close.

130 says அறம் itself watches for the right moment and enters the path of one who has guarded against anger, learned, and is restrained (அறம் பார்க்கும் ஆற்றின் நுழைந்து); 204 says that if you plot another's ruin, அறம் plots the ruin of the plotter (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). In both verses virtue is an agent that acts on a person, seeking out the restrained and planning against the malicious.

130 has virtue looking for its chance and coming along the path to the restrained person; 594 has prosperity asking the way and going to the one of unwavering energy (ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும்). The same figure, a good that seeks out the person fit for it instead of being pursued, is used for virtue in the first book and for worldly gain in the second. The edition's text of 594 has lost its first letter (க்கம் for ஆக்கம்), but the reading is not in doubt.

131 says conduct is to be guarded more than life because it gives excellence (ஒழுக்கம் உயிரினும் ஓம்பப்படும்); 1017 says those ruled by shame will give up life for shame and will not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்). Both place a quality of character above life itself; 1017 states as what such people actually do what 131 states as a rule.

131 ranks conduct above one's own life; 327 says do not do the deed that takes another's life even if your own life should go (தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும் செய்யற்க). The 'more than life' ranking is applied to conduct in general in one verse and to the single act of not killing in the other.

132 says guard conduct with effort, for however much one sifts and examines, it alone is the help (தெரிந்தோம்பித் தேரினும் அஃதே துணை); 242 says hold to அருள், for by whatever many ways one examines, it alone is the help (பல்லாற்றால் தேரினும் அஃதே துணை). The closing words are the same, with the exclusive அஃதே, applied to conduct in the householder's section and to அருள் in the ascetic's; read together, each stage of life is told that its own central virtue is what survives every inquiry.

133 says having conduct is what good family is, and a lapse becomes low birth (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை இழுக்கம் இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்); 972 says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction differs by the difference in what they do (பிறப்பொக்கும் ... செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான்). Both move rank from birth to action. Parimelazhagar reads 133 inside the system of வருணம், as conduct proper to each class, which is narrower than the bare Tamil.

133 makes conduct the thing that constitutes good family (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை); 951 says integrity and shame are found together by nature only in those born in a good house (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்அல்லது இல்லை இயல்பாக). If குடிமை in 133 means that conduct alone makes one well-born, 951 runs the other way and makes birth the source of the conduct. The conflict disappears on Parimelazhagar's reading of 133, where conduct only preserves or forfeits a rank that birth has already given.

133 says a lapse from conduct turns into low birth; 1019 says a lapse in கொள்கை burns one's lineage (குலஞ்சுடும் கொள்கை பிழைப்பின்), and Parimelazhagar glosses கொள்கை there as ஒழுக்கம். Both say family standing is lost through the individual's failure in conduct, one calling the result a low birth and the other a burning.

134 says a Brahmin can relearn the Veda he has forgotten, but his birth is ruined when conduct declines (பார்ப்பான் பிறப்பொழுக்கம் குன்றக் கெடும்); 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous, because they live clothed in kindness to all beings (செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுகலான்). Both tie the title to how the person lives and not to learning or descent. Parimelazhagar takes அந்தணர் in 30 to mean renouncers, so on his reading the two verses concern different people.

134 treats forgetting the Veda (மறப்பினும் ஓத்துக் கொளலாகும்) as a loss that can be made good; 560 lists among the effects of a king who does not protect that those of the six occupations forget their books (அறுதொழிலோர் நூல்மறப்பர்). The same forgetting appears as a private, repairable lapse in 134 and as a sign of public ruin in 560, while 134 keeps conduct as the loss that cannot be repaired.

135 argues by comparison: as there is no gain in the envious, there is no elevation in one without conduct (அழுக்காறுடையான்கண் ஆக்கம் போன்று இல்லை). 170 states the premise on its own: none have grown great through envy (அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை). 135 takes chapter 17's claim as already known and builds its point about conduct on it.

135 takes it as given that the envious have no gain (ஆக்கம்); 169 says the gain of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright are things to be pondered (அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கமும் ... நினைக்கப்படும்). 169 concedes that the case 135 calls non-existent can occur and needs explaining, which weakens the simile's premise; Parimelazhagar softens it by adding 'if they occur'.

136 says the strong do not slacken in conduct, knowing the harm that comes of a lapse (இழுக்கத்தின் ஏதம் படுபாக்கறிந்து); 164 says people do no wrong out of envy, knowing the harm that comes of the wrong path (இழுக்காற்றின் ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து). The second lines are nearly the same words, and both verses ground good behaviour in foreseeing consequences, which 136 counts as strength (உரவோர்).

137 says that from conduct people reach high standing and from a lapse they reach எய்தாப் பழி, which Parimelazhagar takes as blame that is not properly theirs, laid on them because the lapse makes it believable. 117 says the world will not count as ruin the low state of one who stays in the right by being fair (கெடுவாக வையாது உலகம்). In both the world's verdict follows character more than facts: it discounts the upright person's fall and charges the lapsed person with more than he did.

138 calls good conduct the seed of good (நன்றிக்கு வித்தாகும் நல்லொழுக்கம்) and says bad conduct always gives suffering; 361 calls craving the seed that produces unending birth for all beings (தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து). The seed figure is used for a cause whose yield comes later and keeps coming, once for a good crop and once for a bad one.

139 says speaking evil things even by a slip is not possible for those who have conduct (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல் ஒல்லாவே); 199 says those of stainless sight do not say meaningless things even in forgetfulness (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லார்). Both claim that a settled quality rules out even the accidental lapse of speech, and they trace that quality to conduct in one case and to clear understanding in the other.

139 says a person of conduct cannot speak evil even by a slip; 1044 says that even in the well-born, poverty brings the slackness from which degrading words are born (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும் இன்மை இளிவந்த சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு தரும்). 1044 names a condition, want, under which the slip of speech that 139 calls impossible does happen to good people.

139 makes the absence of evil speech a test of having conduct; 959 says that as a sprout shows the ground it lay in, the words from the mouth show the family of the one born in it (குலத்தில் பிறந்தார் வாய்ச்சொல்). Both treat what comes out of the mouth as the evidence of what a person is.

140 says those who have not learned to live in accord with the world (உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்) lack understanding, however much they have studied; 426 says that to live with the world as the world lives is understanding (உலகத்தோடு அவ்வது உறைவது அறிவு). 140 states negatively in the first book what 426 states positively in the second, and both define அறிவு by fit with the world and not by study.

140 says much study without the ability to live in accord with the world is not understanding; 637 tells the minister that even after knowing the method of doing a thing, he must act knowing the way of the world (உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்). 637 applies 140's ranking of worldly fit over book-knowledge to practical statecraft; Parimelazhagar glosses செயற்கை there as methods learned from treatises.

140 makes accord with the world the test that learning must pass; 280 says neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்துவிடின்). In both, the world's standard outranks a formal qualification, learning for the scholar and outward marks for the ascetic. Parimelazhagar takes உலகம் in both verses as the worthy and not people at large.
